nutshell: Deploying person ReID on edge devices at different resource budgets normally means running a separate compression (pruning or distillation) pass per target model size. OSKT instead compresses a teacher model's knowledge once into an intermediate 'weight chain' - same depth as the teacher but a much narrower width - obtained by clustering the teacher's weight rows and jointly refining the teacher with a matching small 'S-Student'. Once built, the weight chain can be expanded to any width between its own and the teacher's, instantly and with zero extra training, by proportionally stacking and merging rows.
contributions: The 'weight chain' concept: an intermediate knowledge carrier with the teacher's full depth but a drastically reduced width, initialized by clustering the teacher's weight rows per layer (cluster centers become the chain's rows) so that a student model of any width between the chain's width and the teacher's can be generated via proportional row-stacking plus normalization-parameter merging - an O(1) operation requiring no additional training per target size.

Progressive refinement: jointly trains the teacher model and the smallest possible 'S-Student' (matching the chain's width) using standard ReID losses (ID + triplet) plus an MSE 'refining loss' that pulls weight-chain rows toward their corresponding teacher-row cluster, so gradients from both ends of this 'bridge' implicitly improve every intermediate-width student without training them directly.

A unified row/column abstraction for weight matrices that treats CNN filters and ViT weight-matrix rows the same way, letting one method apply across both architecture families as well as lightweight backbones (OSNet, MSINet).

Empirical gains over training from scratch, KD++ distillation, DepGraph pruning, and Weight Selection across single-scenario transfer (Market1501), three cross-scenario transfer settings (MSMT17→Market1501/CUHK03, Market1501→CUHK03), few-shot settings, and when combined with lightweight OSNet/MSINet backbones - while needing only one round of teacher+S-Student training regardless of how many target sizes (k) are ultimately required.
deficiencies: The 'one-shot, no additional computation' framing understates the real training cost: OSKT still requires fully training the teacher model plus an S-Student for as many epochs as a traditional method would spend on a single model (Table 5: '100·m' or '120·m' epochs). The savings only materialize once more than a handful of target sizes (k) are actually needed, but every results table compares against k=6 (ResNet) or k=2 (ViT) target sizes without ever showing where the crossover point is for smaller k.

The scalability analysis (Fig. 7, Sec 4.4.2) shows a single weight chain degrades once the required size range gets wide enough that multiple chains (m>1) are needed to preserve performance - but the main results tables (1-4) never state how many chains (m) were actually used to cover their widest reported ranges (e.g. the 32x parameter span from Res-50-S1 to S6), making the 'one-shot' claim hard to verify at the largest tested spans without digging into the appendix.

Table 5 reports the differing epoch budgets across methods (WTSel needs no knowledge-transfer epochs at all; KD++ needs 200·k; DepGraph and OSKT need 100·k / 100·m respectively) in a separate table from the accuracy comparisons in Tables 3-4, making it easy to read those accuracy numbers as apples-to-apples when the underlying training budgets per method actually differ substantially.

Ablation Table 7 shows that removing progressive refinement entirely ('w/o refinement', row (e)) - i.e., just using teacher-weight clustering for initialization with no further joint training - still beats scratch training by a wide margin (e.g. ViT-S-S1: 56.6 vs. 13.9 mAP on Market1501). This means a substantial share of OSKT's total advantage comes from the clustering-based initialization alone, not from the progressive refinement training the paper positions as a central contribution.
notable: The 'neural identity transformation' insight (Fig. 3a) - that merging identical weight rows and correspondingly summing their next-layer columns exactly preserves a network's function when those rows are truly redundant - is a clean, reusable mathematical justification for why proportional row-stacking can approximate the teacher's behavior without retraining. It's effectively the mechanism that makes 'expand a small chain into a bigger model for free' work at all, and could plausibly be reused for compression/scaling problems well beyond ReID.
